newsitem.title: USA: More FBI agents added to tobacco industry probe.
newsitem.headline: More FBI agents added to tobacco industry probe.

text.p: More FBI agents recently were added to the Justice Department's wide-ranging criminal investigation into the tobacco industry, department officials said on Thursday.

The officials were unable to detail how many FBI agents were assigned to the investigation into allegations that the tobacco industry and its top executives withheld information and lied to Congress and federal agencies.
The officials, however, said the agents were added several weeks ago, and that the investigation, led by the Justice Department's fraud section, was moving forward.
One official specifically denied that a special FBI task force had been created. "That is overhyped. FBI agents have been involved from the beginning," he said.
The investigation also is looking into allegations that heads of the major cigarette companies committed perjury when they testified before Congress in 1994 that nicotine was not addictive.
The officials said the long-running probe had not been expanded, but that additional FBI agents had been needed to help carry out the investigation, including reviewing newly available documents.

"The case involves millions of pages of documents," one official said. The department is reviewing internal documents from Liggett Group Inc., which agreed to make the documents available as part of its settlement of lawsuits filed by 22 states.

CBS News reported on Thursday it had exclusive information that a federal law-enforcement task force was working on the first major case involving possible criminal charges against top cigarette industry executives and their lawyers.
The officials declined comment on whether any charges may be brought soon.

According to CBS and other news media reports, a former Philip Morris Cos. research chief, Thomas Osdene, has become the first tobacco executive to exercise his right not to incriminate himself in testimony in a tobacco lawsuit.

Asked at her weekly news briefing if any tobacco industry officials had been seeking immunity, Attorney General Janet Reno said, "I would not comment." Reno has a longstanding policy of declining comment on pending criminal probes.
But a Justice Department official said Osdene's testimony reportedly took place in connection with a civil lawsuit by the state of Texas, not with the federal investigation.
